sites.name: Pasargadae
sites.bodyHtml:
Pasargadae, in the highlands of Fars, was the first Achaemenid capital.

But Pasargadae’s enduring monument is the tomb of Cyrus: a simple, dignified gabled stone chamber raised on six broad steps, standing alone on the plain.

excerpts.html: Pasargadae, in the highlands of Fars, was the first Achaemenid capital.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: Pasargadae, in the highlands of Fars, was the first Achaemenid capital. Cyrus the Great founded it on the site of his victory over the Medes. Its scattered palaces, gardens, and columned halls introduced ideas the later capitals would magnify — including the walled royal paradise garden (see Section 03). But Pasargadae’s enduring monument is the tomb of Cyrus: a simple, dignified gabled stone chamber raised on six broad steps, standing alone on the plain. Why does it survive? Largely because, centuries later, Alexander the Great is said to have ordered it protected and restored — honoring the founder even as he ended the dynasty. That plain limestone tomb is the resting place of the man Isaiah called the LORD’s “shepherd” and “anointed” (see Section 05) — the deliverer who ended the exile. Its restraint is itself a kind of eloquence.

sites.name: Persepolis
sites.bodyHtml:
Persepolis (Old Persian Parsa) was the empire’s great ceremonial capital. Darius the Great began it; Xerxes and their successors expanded it.

It was also where the Persepolis Fortification tablets were found (see Section 08).

excerpts.html: Persepolis (Old Persian Parsa) was the empire’s great ceremonial capital. Darius the Great began it; Xerxes and their successors expanded it.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: Persepolis (Old Persian Parsa) was the empire’s great ceremonial capital. Darius the Great began it; Xerxes and their successors expanded it. Picture a vast terraced complex of audience halls, palaces, and a treasury, approached by monumental stairways. This was where the kings celebrated the New Year and received the empire. It was also where the Persepolis Fortification tablets were found (see Section 08).

sites.name: Naqsh-e Rustam
sites.bodyHtml: Naqsh-e Rustam: a short distance from Persepolis lies the cliff-face burial ground (necropolis) of Naqsh-e Rustam, holding the rock-cut tombs of Darius the Great and several successors.

excerpts.html: Naqsh-e Rustam: a short distance from Persepolis lies the cliff-face burial ground (necropolis) of Naqsh-e Rustam, holding the rock-cut tombs of Darius the Great and several successors.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: Naqsh-e Rustam: a short distance from Persepolis lies the cliff-face burial ground (necropolis) of Naqsh-e Rustam, holding the rock-cut tombs of Darius the Great and several successors. Each tomb is a huge cross-shaped facade carved into the cliff, showing the king worshipping before a fire altar under the winged emblem of Ahura Mazda (see Section 04). Darius’s tomb inscription there is one of the noblest statements of Achaemenid kingship. It presents the king as a just ruler — one who rewards the faithful, punishes the wrongdoer, and holds the sprawling empire together by law.

sites.name: Susa / Shushan
sites.bodyHtml: Susa — the “Shushan” of the Bible — was the administrative and winter capital, on the warm lowland plains. Excavations uncovered the great columned audience hall (apadana) of Darius and Xerxes, along with the glazed-brick reliefs of royal guards. By tradition, Susa is also home to a shrine revered as the tomb of Daniel, honored by Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike. For the court, and for Esther, Nehemiah and Daniel at Susa, see Section 07.

sites.name: Ecbatana / Achmetha
sites.bodyHtml:
Ecbatana (biblical Achmetha) was the old Median capital, high in the Zagros mountains — modern Hamadan. It served as the Achaemenids’ cool summer residence.

Cyrus’s decree found filed here (Ezra 6:2)

excerpts.html: Ecbatana (biblical Achmetha) was the old Median capital, high in the Zagros mountains — modern Hamadan. It served as the Achaemenids’ cool summer residence.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: Ecbatana (biblical Achmetha) was the old Median capital, high in the Zagros mountains — modern Hamadan. It served as the Achaemenids’ cool summer residence. And it earns its biblical moment in one of the most satisfying scenes in Ezra. The Jews’ opponents challenge their permit to rebuild. Darius orders a search of the archives. And Cyrus’s original decree is found — not in Babylon, but filed away at Ecbatana: “there was found at Achmetha, in the palace… a roll, and therein was a record thus written” (Ezra 6:2). It was the exact document, in the exact kind of provincial archive, that vindicated the whole enterprise (see Section 06). The detail that the decree turned up at the summer capital, where Cyrus may well have been residing when he issued it, is the kind of incidental precision that marks a writer who knew the empire’s workings.

sites.bodyHtml: On the mountain road between Babylon and Ecbatana rises the Behistun cliff. There Darius the Great carved his trilingual monument of victory (see Section 08).

excerpts.html: On the mountain road between Babylon and Ecbatana rises the Behistun cliff. There Darius the Great carved his trilingual monument of victory (see Section 08).
excerpts.originalElementHtml: On the mountain road between Babylon and Ecbatana rises the Behistun cliff. There Darius the Great carved his trilingual monument of victory (see Section 08). Behistun names no biblical figure. It belongs on any list of the empire’s great sites anyway — both as the fullest statement of Achaemenid royal ideology and as the “Rosetta Stone of cuneiform” that reopened the writing of the entire ancient Near East to the modern world.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.bodyHtml: The first returnees under Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel rebuilt the altar and laid the temple’s foundation within a couple of years (Ezra 3:8–10). Then the work stalled — for about fifteen years.

excerpts.html: The first returnees under Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel rebuilt the altar and laid the temple’s foundation within a couple of years (Ezra 3:8–10). Then the work stalled — for about fifteen years.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: The first returnees under Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel rebuilt the altar and laid the temple’s foundation within a couple of years (Ezra 3:8–10). Then the work stalled — for roughly fifteen years. Local peoples, rebuffed when they offered to help build (Ezra 4:1–5), “weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building,” hiring counselors to frustrate the project. Discouragement and hard times did the rest; the people turned to their own houses and let God’s house lie waste.

sites.name: Samaria
sites.bodyHtml:
In a petition dated 407 BC, the priests of Elephantine asked Bagohi, the governor of Judah, for help rebuilding their temple, which had been destroyed in 410 BC.

They had already appealed to Jerusalem’s high priest without receiving an answer, and also wrote to the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. This was an established temple community seeking help through the same religious and political networks that appear in Ezra and Nehemiah.

sites.name: Nazareth
sites.note: This pin accompanies the guide’s later language comparison; it is not a Persian-period event.
sites.bodyHtml: And the story runs further still. The Jews carried this Aramaic home, and it remained the daily speech of Judea for centuries — so that the language of the Persian bureaucracy became, in time, the mother tongue of Jesus of Nazareth.

excerpts.html: And the story runs further still. The Jews carried this Aramaic home, and it remained the daily speech of Judea for centuries — so that the language of the Persian bureaucracy became, in time, the mother tongue of Jesus of Nazareth.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: This is why the Bible itself goes bilingual in exactly the Persian-document sections. The books of Ezra reproduce official correspondence in Aramaic — the accusation letter to Artaxerxes and his reply, the exchange with Darius, and Artaxerxes’s commission to Ezra (Ezra 4:8–6:18; 7:12–26). The text preserves the documents in the very language they were issued in, then switches back to Hebrew for the narrative. Portions of Daniel are likewise in Aramaic. Far from a defect, this bilingual texture is a mark of authenticity: the compilers had real Persian-era documents in hand and quoted them as they stood. And the story runs further still. The Jews carried this Aramaic home, and it remained the daily speech of Judea for centuries — so that the language of the Persian bureaucracy became, in time, the mother tongue of Jesus of Nazareth.

sites.name: Elephantine
sites.bodyHtml:
Jerusalem was not the only place where Jews worshipped Israel’s God in a temple. At Elephantine, near modern Aswan in Egypt, a Jewish military community left Aramaic letters, contracts, and records of family and religious life. Its sanctuary was dedicated to Yahu, a form of the name Yahweh.

In a petition dated 407 BC, its priests asked Bagohi, the governor of Judah, for help rebuilding their temple, which had been destroyed in 410 BC.

sites.name: Sardis
sites.bodyHtml: An empire that large lived or died by communication. So Persia built and maintained the Royal Road — a highway running some 2,700 kilometers from Susa in the heartland to Sardis near the Aegean coast, with about 111 posting-stations a day’s ride apart, each stocked with fresh horses and riders.

excerpts.html: An empire that large lived or died by communication. So Persia built and maintained the Royal Road — a highway running some 2,700 kilometers from Susa in the heartland to Sardis near the Aegean coast, with about 111 posting-stations a day’s ride apart, each stocked with fresh horses and riders.
excerpts.originalElementHtml: An empire that large lived or died by communication. So Persia built and maintained the Royal Road — a highway running some 2,700 kilometers from Susa in the heartland to Sardis near the Aegean coast, with about 111 posting-stations a day’s ride apart, each stocked with fresh horses and riders. Think about what that meant. A royal courier, riding the relay, could carry a message the length of that road in about nine days. An ordinary traveler needed three months. Herodotus, the Greek historian who traveled the Persian world a generation later, left a famous description of these couriers — that neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor darkness stayed them from their rounds. He was describing this Persian postal relay (the line later became the unofficial motto of the U.S. Postal Service).

sites.name: Gaugamela
sites.bodyHtml: Alexander the Great destroys the empire — Darius III defeated at Gaugamela (the battle that ended the empire), Persepolis burned. This is the age Daniel foresaw as the “he goat… from the west” (Daniel 8:5), interpreted as “the king of Grecia” (Daniel 8:21)
